In InSiGHT they caught their own pipeline's instability - mutating key polar residues to alanine did not abolish predicted binding as it should, and one HADDOCK run gave mutant Gamma -6.495 kcal/mol against Core 1 while a separate run of the same mutant gave -3.84, which they report as evidence the pipeline needs repeated runs. For VOIR they state the point is the optimal linker length range, not the headline avidity ratio, because the values are literature-derived estimates not validated in vitro. For HOPE the model behaved as theory predicts (mesh falling from 16 nm at 5% w/v PEGDA to about 10 nm at 25%, predicted protein diffusivity from about 60 to 37 micrometres squared per second against 97 in free water) and they say plainly they could not build the equivalent alginate model, and that an OpenFOAM CFD attempt failed because the corneal absorption boundary condition had to be written in C++ and did not run reliably, so they fell back to a 1D Python model for sensitivity analysis.

**dataviz.** The modelling page is organised as a relay: five labelled operations (Choose, Improve, Multiply, Produce, Deliver) in a flow a reader clicks into, each with its own write-up and its own Impressiveness/Design/Validation/Exemplarity framing. The software page embeds a live in-browser CLI simulator for GLARE with clickable example commands (--cell eye, --binding-galectins eye, --target-compare eye core1 stn, --disease-compare dry_eye) so a judge can run the pipeline's logic without installing Python. For audiences without a biology background the team built the gleyecobuddies: Lecto (Galectin-3, with the binding site built into the character design), Ana (IL-1RA, a red plus sign) and Happy (HABpep, a blue rectangle standing for a wall that holds the drug in place), deliberately layered on top of the standard Symbol Nomenclature for Glycans rather than replacing it, and justified as serving visual learners, neurodivergent people and children. All InSiGHT results are reported with the predictors' disagreements visible rather than averaged.

**software.** GLARE, released as an importable Python package (v0.2.0, Python 3.10+) at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/ualberta/software-glare, runnable from the command line with a clear module structure separating tissue validation, binding analysis, cross-tissue comparison, disease signatures and docking-structure generation behind a single pipeline interface, with generalised inputs so another team can point it at a different tissue, lectin or glycan. A browser-based CLI simulator on the wiki lets anyone try it without installing. The Adaptive Technology Kit is an open-source hardware release: 3D-printable PCR strip-tube and microfuge-tube openers (in multiple design variants, because user testing showed different researchers preferred different models), an agarose gel loader, an SDS gel loader, a braille stamper, a keyboard tool, a pencil holder, a non-slip tray, a microscope phone holder, and a tactile map of the iGEM lab with published blueprints. A Synthetic Biology Lab Manual and the full Rural Teachers Synbiosium materials are published as free PDFs, as is the DNA-as-Code Kit.

**ihp.** Every stakeholder entry is logged as a Key Insight paired with an Action Taken, and the actions are real design reversals. Dr Warren Wakarchuk (Scientific Director of GlycoNet) warned that small-molecule binding pockets hold cargo too tightly to release on the eye and that yeast adds problematic sugar tags, and noted eukaryotic tissue autofluoresces green under UV - so the team abandoned the binding-pocket release concept, chose E. coli over yeast, switched the reporter from GFP to mScarlet, and retargeted abundant normal ocular glycans instead of rare disease-specific ones. Dr Lisa Willis (glyco-immunology) raised immune safety and challenged them to test whether the Galectin-3 and HA domains cooperate or compete for binding - so instead of assuming more binding is better, they redesigned the experimental plan to measure each domain separately by isothermal titration calorimetry. Dr Carr advised narrowing from retinal delivery to corneal inflammation in dry eye with IL-1RA cargo and offered Xenopus eye tissue for ex vivo testing. An advisor recommended the SHuffle T7 strain and told them their fusion protein was not complex enough to justify a chaperone plasmid, so they dropped it. Dr Amandeep helped unify the five separate models into one pipeline and suggested using eye images as GLARE input to make it diagnostic - the team pursued it, found it infeasible, said so, and redirected to modelling; he also pointed them to RunPod, which is why FoldX now runs in parallel. Jezlyn warned that chemical and UV crosslinking would denature mScarlet, so they moved to physical ionic crosslinking with calcium chloride, wrote autoclaving protocols for sterility, and were pointed at the Peppas-Merrill and Flory-Rehner equations that became HOPE. Dr Cortez told them not to add a second nickel column but to optimise their existing HisTrap/FPLC wash stringency, which they did and documented on Coomassie gels. Optometrist Dr Abdo Kattan explained that his multi-product dry eye package (omega 3s, drops, lid wipes, goggles) has very low compliance because it is time-consuming, expensive and impossible to attribute benefit to - which refocused the whole project on one affordable single-product treatment. Separately, CD44 was dropped entirely as the HA-retention domain in favour of tandem HABpep after it kept appearing in the insoluble fraction and the literature revealed isoforms linked to cancer therapy resistance. On the inclusivity side, Nicholas Piroddi (a medical researcher with autism) was consulted, then consulted a second time to review how the course represented neurodiversity, which added the institutional reporting-pathways module; ASVI's input became the blind and visually impaired module; and user testing of the 3D-printed tube openers at the WinSTEM expo is why the kit ships multiple variants of the same tool.

**publicEngagement.** Three distinct, durable programmes rather than one-off booths. (1) The Inclusivity in Research Course, an open-access training run through Google Classroom, built from a nationwide survey and expert consultations, with modules on a Native Land activity, the team's own 'Just Ask' framework and neurodivergent inclusion, creating open spaces, blind and visually impaired inclusion, Deaf and hard-of-hearing inclusion, racialized people, women and 2SLGBTQIA+ and gender minorities, navigating reporting processes, and an accessibility resource bank - each with downloadable slides, infographics and interactive summaries. It was piloted with their own team, neighbouring labs and Canadian iGEM teams, and the three pieces of pilot feedback (offer multiple learning formats, add scenario-based practice, cover more groups) were each implemented as narrated audio and slideshows, self-reflection prompts and real lab case studies, and two new modules. (2) The Rural Teachers Synbiosium, a half-day online professional development event for rural Alberta teachers, mapped explicitly onto the Alberta middle and high school curriculum, covering case studies and how to secure funding, with three guest speakers including Amino Labs CEO Julie Legault, 9 free hands-on kits distributed (teachers chose between a one-day yeast-fermentation race car and a multi-day pigment-engineering agar art project) and all materials shipped in advance to lower the burden. (3) Public outreach at K-Days, an Edmonton summer festival, where visitors attempted lab tasks while simulating different visual impairments, plus a DNA-as-code bracelet activity, and tabling at Alberta's Women in STEM week after being invited by the Alberta Women in Science Network. The team also presented at the Canadian Glycomics Symposium, CNAS Research Day, Darwin Day, Cell Biology Research Day, the RE Peter Conference and the Canadian iGEM GCI Conference, and ran a hands-on workshop at Canmore Collegiate High School - which is what revealed the rural access problem and started the Synbiosium.

**realWorld.** The strongest undergraduate commercial case of the five. Evidence of demand is tabulated by customer role with the strength of evidence named: letters of support from Dr Abdo Kattan and Dr Matthew Benson (and a signed letter of intent from Kattan's clinic to work with them), 86% of 38 surveyed dry eye patients interested in a synthetic biology treatment, and an application in interview stage with the Nucleate Canada accelerator. The patient survey plus three clinician interviews produced five explicit unmet needs - fewer doses, longer retention, no burning or stinging, targeted anti-inflammatory action, contact lens compatibility - which the product is then measured against. A competitor matrix compares gleyeco line by line with Restasis (AbbVie), Cequa (Sun Pharma) and Xiidra (Bausch + Lomb) on mechanism, dosing, time to effect, clinical evidence, tolerability, lens compatibility, 30-day cost and Canadian availability, citing prescribing information and Drugs.com prices as of 15 October 2026, and crucially labels gleyeco's own entries as design goals that preclinical and clinical data must confirm. The gap identified is precise: every anti-inflammatory option is dosed at least twice daily and none occupies targeted once-daily treatment. TAM/SAM/SOM, regional opportunity, bottom-up dynamics, current distribution network, a Size-Potential-Access analysis, a beachhead market defined by role (users, decision makers, payers, pharmaceutical partners), a 10-year implementation plan and an exit strategy all follow. The PESTEL analysis is specific to Canadian biotech: Health Canada's Reliance Order syncing review with the FDA if filed within 120 days, Alberta Innovates and FAST cutting trial start-up from 90+ to 45 days, PMPRB price controls pushing them toward private payers first, over 75% of Canadian life-science investment coming from abroad so Phase 2 needs a partner, the USD/CAD rate at 1.4, and the fact that the RE Peter Conference and Jamboree disclosures start the novelty clock (12 months in Canada, absolute novelty required in Europe). Clinical milestones were set directly from a clinician's roadmap, and lab eye models have been offered by two separate researchers for the move from proof of concept to preclinical.

**給 GEMS：** Copy UAlberta's two-column human practices habit - every conversation written as one Key Insight and one Action Taken, where the action is a concrete reversal (GFP to mScarlet, yeast to E. coli, CD44 dropped for HABpep, chemical crosslinking dropped for calcium) - because it forces a team to admit when advice changed nothing. The other directly adaptable asset is their rural pivot: they went in planning to help schools found competition teams, learned from the teachers that capacity was the real constraint, and instead built a curriculum-aligned half-day online session with pre-shipped kits and a free lab manual, which is exactly the model a Taiwanese research centre could run for under-resourced schools.

### UOttawa — Nulfur
Undergrad · Canada · https://2026.igem.wiki/uottawa/
Nulfur 把源自 Rhodococcus erythropolis 的四酶 4S 生物脫硫途徑（DszA、DszB、DszC 加上一個黃素還原酶）重建於 Pseudomonas putida KT2440 之中，標的是二苯并噻吩（DBT），也就是傳統加氫脫硫必須在 300-400 C、3-6 MPa 條件下才勉強能處理的難脫除硫化物。團隊在與業界諮詢後，並未把專案定位為取代加氫脫硫，而是重新定義為柴油上的模組化側流精製步驟。本專案的獲獎實力來自替代底盤的工作：由於 P. putida 屬於非模式生物，團隊從零建立起原本缺乏的工具組（一個相容於 Golden Gate 的廣宿主範圍載體、一組經過量測的四啟動子系列，以及一套可用的熱休克轉型流程），並把它整理成供其他團隊使用的手冊。這項平台貢獻，搭配一個深度罕見的乾實驗（COBRApy 基因組尺度代謝模型、FoldX/ThermoMPNN 蛋白質工程流程，以及名為 Cofactor 的代理式 AI 研究平台），為團隊贏得 Best Alternative Platform，並入圍 Best Wiki 與 Best Bioremediation Project。

**frameworks.** 三個不同的計算層次。(1) 基因組尺度代謝模型：團隊在 COBRApy 中把已發表的 P. putida KT2440 模型 iJN1463 擴充，加入異源 4S 途徑的反應（DszA/B/C/D），並以 GLPK 求解通量平衡分析，對 DBT 交換通量上限做 1000 點掃描，結果顯示代謝從未成為攝取的瓶頸；而強制給定 DszB 通量後，則揭露出一個受 NADH 限制的上限 9.80 mmol gDCW-1 h-1，共餵入甲酸可將此上限提高 25.5% 至 12.30。(2) 雙相反應器的第一原理質傳模型，結合 Hinze-Kolmogorov 液滴破裂尺度律、停滯球極限下的薄膜理論（Sh = 2）、CMC 以上的微胞增溶，以及 Michaelis-Menten 型攝取，並以二分法求解穩態的游離 DBT 濃度；模型預測鼠李糖脂可讓有效的 DBT 可得量提高 2.8 至 34 倍。(3) 一條蛋白質工程流程，以 ConSurf 保守性等級、由分子動力學模擬得到的主鏈 RMSF，以及 FoldX（經驗力場）加上 ThermoMPNN（在 ProteinMPNN 嵌入向量上做深度學習）的集成來估算 ddG，篩選 DszB 與 DszC 中超過 1,100 個候選取代；接著以顯式溶劑的 GROMACS 分子動力學模擬（amber99sb-ildn、TIP3P）與 AutoDock Vina 配體對接驗證催化功能是否完好，最後為每個酶挑出五個突變體入選名單。

**datascience.** 最突出的資料科學貢獻，是把蛋白質工程的迭代迴圈變成一個可量測、可稽核的產出。團隊為 Cofactor 建立了六組評估套件，含四種消融（ablation）設定（bare、bare_prompt、tools、full），每一種剛好多加一層外框機制，然後對結果評分：A、B 兩組中 37 項確定性探測全數通過；C 組在階段狀態機之下，27 次可評分執行中記錄到零次流程違規，而在 bare 條件下為兩次；D 組則發現未加接地的條件會虛構出胺基酸位置，而兩種有接地的條件都沒有。E 組要求代理重建六篇已發表論文的初始實驗設計（其中三篇發表於模型知識截止日之後），並稽核工具的操作紀錄以檢查是否受到汙染。濕實驗方面，啟動子庫以每 OD600 的 mScarlet-i 螢光取對數歸一化後定量，並扣除培養基背景與 P. putida 自體螢光，結果顯示只有三個明顯的表現量層級，而非文獻報告中的四個。

**dataviz.** 這個 wiki 是一個讀起來像伺服器渲染的 React 網站，視覺層確實經過工程設計：首頁有以 WebGL/Three.js 製作的蒸餾塔場景與動畫化的途徑迴圈；每一條方程式都各自渲染成帶標註的 SVG，使整段推導讀起來像一條連貫的鏈；預測器一致性散布圖（圖 9）則把 FoldX 與 ThermoMPNN 同時判定該取代具穩定化效果的象限加上底色，並將該象限放大，標示出實際送進實驗台的五個突變。人類實踐頁面做成可點選的堆疊柱狀圖，每一段代表 21 筆紀錄中七類對話之一，讓評審可以直接跳到自己關心的利害關係人族群。每張圖都附有長篇描述性的 alt 屬性，寫出該圖實際的數值，而不只是它的主題。

**software.** Cofactor 是一個代理式蛋白質工程平台，以 MIT 授權釋出於 https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/uottawa/cofactor。它把一個通用 LLM 包在一個明確的階段狀態機之中，各階段的前置條件是對照一個 16 張表的 SQLite 資料庫（.cofactor/research.sqlite3，WAL 日誌、外鍵）來檢查，而不是採信模型自己的說法，因此執行可以跨工作階段續跑，研究紀錄也不必依賴這個工具就能讀懂。確定性的工具層涵蓋序列操作、RFC10 相容性檢查、密碼子最佳化、限制酶切位分析、溶解度掃描，以及從 UniProt、NCBI、RCSB PDB、AlphaFold、PubMed 與 Europe PMC 擷取資料；ExecutionManager 則負責把運算工作送往本機、SSH 或 Slurm 後端。平台提供三種前端：FastAPI 網頁介面、Textual TUI 與 CLI，全部採自備金鑰、不限模型，可對接任何 OpenAI 相容端點。團隊同時釋出了 P. putida 手冊（含實驗流程）以及經過整理、可直接用於 Golden Gate 的 pBBR1MCS-2 載體至 iGEM Registry。

**ihp.** 七個類別、共 21 場對話，每一場都以相同的三段式結構記錄：我們為何去談、我們聽到了什麼、我們改了什麼。這些改動都很具體。Dr. Jinwen Chen（Natural Resources Canada, CanmetENERGY-Devon）與 Dr. Stephen Larter（Calgary，石油地球化學家）都建議團隊放棄重質稀釋瀝青、改做柴油，理由是黏度、質傳與乳化分離上的障礙，以及柴油有硬性的 <10 ppm 含硫上限且難脫除的 DBT 濃度較高，於是團隊把整個目標物流改為柴油精製。Dr. Rasha Maal-Bared 提醒，黏稠原油會以局部層流的方式混合，這一點把靜態混合元件與生物反應器尺寸納入了連續流設計。Patrick Lumley（Safe Sulphur Systems，於硫回收領域有 33 年經驗）指出，水相的亞硫酸鹽副產物需要 pH 控制以避免釋出 SO2，而減輕 Claus 製程負載在經濟上毫無價值，於是 P&ID 中加入了一個 pH 控制迴圈，商業論述也從硫處理量改為重建在節省氫氣與降低加氫處理嚴苛度之上。Larter 對微生物影響腐蝕的提醒，為反應器設計增加了腐蝕與材料相容性的準則。工學院 Design Day 的回饋，則促使團隊從「完全取代 HDS」的敘事轉向互補式的精製模式。團隊還特地向蛋白質化學家 Dr. Corrie DaCosta 請教 Cofactor 的輸出報告必須包含什麼內容，才能讓真正動手做工程的人用得上，報告格式也因此修改。

**publicEngagement.** 教育工作圍繞四項明定原則展開，即觸及（Access）、調適（Adapt）、參與（Engage）、延伸（Extend），每項活動都對應其中一項撰寫成果。團隊在 Ottawa-Carleton District School Board 的 International and Indigenous Languages Program 暑期學校，為 370 位以上 4 至 13 歲兒童舉辦英法雙語課程，又透過 Ottawa Catholic School Board 再觸及 70 人，並造訪 AcadeCap International School 面向 4 至 7 歲學童。原創的動手活動包括 Lava Lamps（油的性質）、The Art of Consortia（以共同創作壁畫類比微生物的分工）、Mix and Match Genes、The Power of Bacterial DNA，以及一份 Heavy vs Light Oil 學習單。為了讓成果能持續，團隊出版了免費的互動式兒童雜誌 Bio-Builder，並明確選擇透過渥太華當地公共圖書館發行，以觸及買不起這類資源的低收入家庭；此外還有示範清單、資訊圖表、一檔科學與研究播客，以及一座可完整下載的資源庫，收錄簡報與學習單，讓這些活動在團隊不在場時也能照樣進行。團隊另主辦了 Great Canadian iGEM Incubator 海報競賽（與 QGEM 合辦）以及 Great Canadian Meetup 提案競賽，兩者都公開了評分量表。

**realWorld.** 一份完整做到底的商業化論證。市場規模：TAM 約 31 億美元（全球 HDS 觸媒市場）、SAM 約 6,600 萬美元（加拿大佔 2.2%，16 座煉油廠，約 200 萬桶/日）、SOM 約 140 萬美元，來自單一煉油廠側流示範，以 10,000 桶/日的物流按每桶 $0.40 收取授權金計算。營收模式為按桶計價的授權金，並在與一位營運與專案工程師的對話中得到驗證。技術經濟分析把 BDS 與 HDS 相比，後者在 20,000 至 25,000 桶/日規模的煉油廠需 1,600 萬至 4,200 萬美元的資本支出，並推估取消高壓氫氣設備可減少 50-60% 資本支出；一份具明確系統邊界並附 BDS/HDS 清單的生命週期評估，支撐了環境效益的說法，而不是只是斷言。分階段時程由概念驗證（2026）、發表論文與申請 NSERC Alliance / Mitacs Accelerate / CRIN 等非稀釋性資金（2027）、以真實進料進行先導示範並依《新物質通報》法規就封閉式 LMO 部署正式向 Environment and Climate Change Canada 進行事前溝通（2028-29），到技術授權（2030 年以後）與擴展至生物脫氮。團隊依 Lumley 的建議，刻意以面臨 Euro V 限值且氫氣產能受限的中小型、老舊煉油廠為目標，而不是大型油砂業者，並指出沼氣生產者是更快取得初期營收的途徑。風險分析、SWOT、商業模式圖（Business Model Canvas）與競爭定位矩陣全部公開，團隊也明白表示 Nulfur 是能源轉型期間的傷害減緩，「一座橋，而非終點」。

**給 GEMS：** 照字面抄下 uOttawa 的人類實踐範本：用單一頁面，把 21 場利害關係人對話全部以相同的三個欄位記錄下來，也就是我們為何去談、我們聽到了什麼、我們改了什麼，而「改了什麼」要寫成具體的設計變更（P&ID 中的一個 pH 控制迴圈、換掉進料、加裝靜態混合器）。採用它不花任何成本，卻能讓學生團隊的推理過程可被稽核，也是一個校內研究中心最清楚的方式，用以證明外部意見確實推動了專案，而不只是拿來裝飾。

### NUS-Singapore — ORCHID
Undergrad · Singapore · https://2026.igem.wiki/nus-singapore/
Industrial bioreactors hold hundreds of thousands of litres and a single bad batch is expensive, yet conventional monitoring tracks only physical and chemical parameters such as pH and dissolved oxygen — nothing about what is happening inside the cell. Omics and LC-MS can see inside, but they are offline, destructive and slow enough that results arrive after the batch has finished, so they cannot act on anything. ORCHID puts biosensors for endoplasmic reticulum, oxidative and ATP stress into Saccharomyces cerevisiae as fluorescent reporters readable straight from a plate reader, solves the resulting spectral overlap with a linear unmixing model, and feeds the separated stress signals into SABLe, a neural-network framework that predicts growth, product and stress from process conditions and then proposes which culture to run next. It won nominations across parts, presentation, wiki and integrated human practices because the loop actually closed: SABLe's exploration rule proposed 27 C, the team grew that plate, and the measured product signal reached 491 mApple RFU/OD600 against 204 and 179 at the 24 and 30 C conditions it was trained on.

**frameworks.** Three layers, built in sequence. First, a linear unmixing model adapted from multispectral fluorescence imaging to plate-reader wells: each sample's readings are modelled as a mixture matrix with one column per reporter and one row per channel, with diagonal entries carrying a reporter's own signal and off-diagonal entries the crosstalk, inverted to recover each reporter's share. It was validated on mixtures of single-reporter strains including untransformed BY4741 for autofluorescence and water-only wells for background, six replicates per condition. Second, a mechanistic baseline: Hill dose-response curves fitted at each temperature for DTT against the stress reporter and galactose against the product reporter, plus simple ODE time-course equations. The ODEs tracked growth well (R-squared about 0.91-0.93) but fitted stress (0.33-0.47) and product (0.41-0.42) poorly, and the team uses that failure as the explicit justification for moving to machine learning rather than assuming ML was needed. Third, SABLe: a multilayer perceptron trained on 700 culture-time records from 40 unique condition combinations (two temperatures at 24 and 30 C, five DTT concentrations 0-1 mM, four galactose concentrations 0-0.2%, three independent plate cultures each, measured at 0, 3, 5, 7, 9 and 24-26 hours), predicting OD600, mApple/OD600 and mCitrine/OD600 without ever receiving their measured values as inputs. On top of the trained network they run gradient ascent (network frozen, 64 starting conditions, 500 steps each, 32,000 evaluations without growing a culture), a ten-member bootstrap ensemble for disagreement-based uncertainty, and UMAP projection of the 64-dimensional latent response to 20,000 queried conditions to inspect what the network learned.

**datascience.** The statistical discipline here is well above the usual standard. Cross-validation groups all biological replicates and time points from a single cultivation condition into one split, because splitting correlated measurements across train and test would inflate performance — so the reported scores (R-squared 0.955 for OD600, 0.891 for mApple/OD600, 0.842 for mCitrine/OD600) measure generalisation to genuinely unseen condition combinations. Channel selection asked how few reads are needed and found one well-chosen channel per reporter matches a full spectral scan (three channels as good as six for three reporters, four as good as eight for four), turning an hour-long scan into minutes so a bioreactor can be sampled routinely. A simulation study set the design rule for adding reporters: for each separation angle from 2 to 90 degrees they generated 3,000 random two-reporter mixtures with 5% noise and found median error stays within 5 percentage points once reporters are at least 28 degrees apart — which is why mCitrine and eGFP at 20 degrees are ruled out. Errors are diagnosed rather than reported: the consistent 3-point overestimate of mTurquoise2 and underestimate of mApple in three-reporter mixtures is attributed to sample preparation rather than the algorithm because noise alone would scatter in both directions, and the larger four-reporter errors are traced to the whole plate being 6-17 times dimmer, leaving mApple and mTurquoise2 only about 160 and 690 RFU above water. Then the model generated a biological hypothesis: UMAP showed conditions with more DTT clustering where both stress and product are predicted high (79% of high-predicted-product conditions were also high DTT, 81% high predicted stress, against 25% expected by chance), the team went back to the measured cultures and confirmed it (Spearman rho, p < 0.001), checked that mCitrine bleed into the mApple channel could explain at most 8% of the rise, and named the next mechanistic question. They also caught their own education-survey analogue of this problem in the model: the 27 C validation plate was read at 24 hours while earlier plates were read at about 25, and they say so.

**dataviz.** The wiki is a Three.js scrollytelling experience that walks a reader from the $2-4 trillion bioeconomy projection down to a single yeast cell, with hoverable bioreactors explaining Titer, Rate and Yield before the project is even introduced — the argument is built visually before any data appears. The dry lab page is laid out as a numbered slide sequence (raw extremes, normalisation, normalised trajectories, stress dose fit, product dose fit, time model fit, fivefold split, held-out scores, held-out trajectories, gradient search, ensemble uncertainty, exploration score, optimisation versus exploration, latent UMAP, measured DTT response, UMAP robustness), so the reasoning chain is the navigation. Two choices stand out. The exploit-versus-explore panel shows side by side that maximising predicted signal just returns to a corner already measured, while the exploration rule spreads eight proposed tests across under-sampled combinations — making the value of the method visible rather than argued. And the UMAP is drawn sixteen different ways with the caption telling the reader to compare colour gradients rather than outlines, with an explicit note that the map axes have no biological units, which is an honest treatment of a technique usually presented as if its shape meant something.

**software.** SABLe and the linear unmixing algorithm are released on the iGEM GitLab at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/software/nus-singapore/model, framed explicitly as a reusable framework rather than a one-project script — future teams can use the unmixing to quantify several fluorescent proteins at once and track multiple cellular processes from a single strain design. The part collection is the other deliverable: 17 modular basic parts (stress-sensing elements including altered and native Yap1 response elements, UPRE1 and UPRE2 Hac1 binding sites, biosensor tuning elements, promoters of differing strengths, terminators, and fluorescent reporters including a genetically encoded green ATP sensor) plus 12 composite parts for the ER, oxidative and ATP stress biosensors, designed for plug-and-play assembly. They also characterised leakiness-reduction design principles as a reusable pattern: Sko1 repression upstream of the TATA box, a cP_CYC1 core promoter to lower basal expression, an ODC degradation tag for continuous turnover of background protein, and an RPP2Bt terminator. Two education artefacts are software: a browser game in which players build genetic circuits in virtual yeast populations, with every number and equation documented by source category (published, game-balance tuned by scripted playtesting, or stated rule) and an honest statement that no value was fitted to a real culture so the game shows the shape of the biology rather than predictions; and SynVision, an app whose camera scanner links everyday objects to synthetic biology concepts and then runs DBTL-guided questioning.

**ihp.** The project's scope was set and then substantially narrowed by stakeholders. An application scientist at TJX Bioengineering established that a single failed batch causes substantial financial loss and shifted the team's attention from the product to the production process and the changing conditions cells experience; Anomaly Bio, a precision fermentation startup, established that conventional monitoring tracks physical and chemical parameters while the cell's inner workings are overlooked because they are hard to measure and hard to interpret. The largest single change came from Dr Bruce Li, Alan Yang and Prof Yong-Su Jin raising scale-up challenges, deployment barriers and startup resource constraints: in response the team moved ORCHID's primary intended application from continuous industrial monitoring to early-stage R&D, naming strain-engineering and process-development teams at startups as the primary users and dropping production-scale deployment as an immediate objective. Several design elements are individually attributable — Dr Jee Loon Foo's guidance set the initial oxidative and ER stress targets, Sheena Chan's feedback added the ATP depletion sensor, and Dr Bruce Li's concerns about whether the biosensors themselves perturb the cell led them to build parental-versus-biosensor-strain comparisons into the experimental design. Sook Wei explained how genome-scale metabolic models represent competition between growth and product formation but warned that conventional metabolic models may not match real cellular behaviour because of unaccounted byproducts, competing pathways and biological constraints, stressing that experimental data is what closes that gap and pointing toward combining genome-scale modelling with machine learning — advice visible in the final architecture, where a mechanistic ODE baseline is fitted first, shown to fail on stress and product, and only then replaced by a learned model. Later feedback also asked them to extend the model to weigh productivity, yield and cost together rather than optimising a single predicted output, which is recorded as future work rather than claimed as done.

**publicEngagement.** NUS treated their educational game as a research object, which is rare at any level. It was designed against Self-Determination Theory with autonomy, competence and relatedness mapped to specific mechanics (free choice of parts, a shared leaderboard, facilitated peer discussion), and every simulation value published with its provenance. Evaluation used paired pre- and post-surveys via Microsoft Forms where participants generated the same anonymous linking code on both forms from details only they would know, so before-and-after answers could be matched without collecting names or emails. They deployed across six settings — Project STEMpact Workshop 3 with secondary school students, NCEB Engineering Biology Week FUTURES Day with polytechnic students, two undergraduate modules (SP2718C and BN4501), NUS Telegram channels and a Raffles Girls' School email blast — getting 58 pre-surveys and 27 post-surveys between 5 September and 18 October 2026, of which 24 paired. The analysis is where it becomes exemplary: four Intrinsic Motivation Inventory subscales were shortened and reworded, then checked for internal consistency with Cronbach's alpha in their own data, which exposed that Perceived Choice at alpha 0.23 was not a single construct (its two items measured having choices and feeling obliged to play) so they reported them separately instead of averaging. Three items were negatively worded and reverse-scored to catch acquiescent responders. Attrition bias was tested — only 41% of pre-survey takers paired — and no item differed (all p > .18). Self-ratings on all three understanding statements rose 1.3-1.8 points (d = 0.76-0.95) and intent to pursue synthetic biology from 4.0 to 4.9 (d = 0.64), all surviving Holm correction. But they also scored free-text definitions as an independent check: promoters rose from 64% to 91% correct, sensors from 23% to 45%, genes stayed at 55%, and the overall written score moved only 1.4 to 1.9 out of 3 (p = .06). Crucially, self-ratings matched written answers before playing (rho = .65) and did not afterwards (rho = -.04) — participants felt they understood more than they could explain — so the team explicitly treats the self-reported gains as an upper bound. Their own headline finding is that participants valued the game more than they enjoyed it: the highest-rated statement in the survey was that the game is useful for understanding synthetic biology (5.5) and the lowest was about enjoying it while playing (4.3).

**realWorld.** The deployment story is deliberately modest after the industry reality check. ORCHID is positioned as an early-stage R&D platform for strain engineering and process development teams at startups, not as production-scale instrumentation, because the team accepted that industrial implementation carries technical and financial constraints they cannot yet meet. The workflow they specify is concrete: build or adopt modular biosensors for the analytes of interest in whatever chassis is being engineered, culture under varied process conditions, train the model on how conditions map to stress responses, use it to interpolate and recommend conditions, then run the organism under those conditions — with the intracellular data also making unintended effects on the host easier to spot. The framing they use for the value proposition is a grey box rather than a black box: in-line pH and dissolved oxygen sensors show how organism and environment affect each other, but when production is inefficient researchers still cannot tell which pathway is the constraint, and high-dimensional intracellular stress data gives a window into that. Because the biosensors are modular, they argue the collection builds toward a shared library: metabolic engineering teams can track the burden a heterologous pathway places on the cell, and environmental synthetic biology teams can assess strain robustness in harsh conditions. Troubleshooting is published as a first-class deliverable, with issues and fixes in segmented boxes down the results page specifically so later teams hit them less hard.

**給 GEMS：** Two things are directly copyable and neither needs a bioreactor. First, NUS's active-learning loop: fit a simple mechanistic model, show where it fails, train a small neural net on your own plate data, then use ensemble disagreement plus distance from tested conditions to pick the next experiment — and actually run it, so the write-up ends with a measured confirmation rather than a prediction. Second, and more unusual, evaluate your outreach the way you evaluate an assay: paired pre/post surveys with anonymous linking codes, reverse-scored items to catch acquiescence, Cronbach's alpha on any scale you shorten, attrition checks, and a free-text knowledge score as an independent check on self-reports. NUS found their participants felt they had learned more than they could explain, and said so — that kind of honesty about one's own teaching is both rare and cheap to adopt.

### UZurich — SeisMIC
Overgrad · Switzerland · https://2026.igem.wiki/uzurich/
SeisMIC adapts microbially induced calcite precipitation (MICP) to Alpine slope stabilisation, where heavy rainfall is now 26% more frequent and 12% more intense and concrete anchoring is often out of proportion to the risk. Sporosarcina pasteurii hydrolyses urea so calcium carbonate crystallises around soil particles, filling pores and binding loose grains, and the team worked on the four limits that stop MICP transferring to the Alps: uneven cementation, scaling across large slopes, cold sensitivity and ammonium production. The distinctive contribution is the dry lab, which is a geospatial and economic decision system rather than a protein pipeline: an infinite-slope Factor of Safety model run across all of Switzerland on daily historical rainfall, a PHREEQC reactive transport model of calcite formation down a soil column, a QGIS MICP feasibility map, and an economic model using Flow-Py runout simulation to put a Swiss franc figure on damage avoided. The models are linked to each other and were reshaped by named expert feedback, which is what earned the Best Model nomination.

**frameworks.** Four models, explicitly chained so each one's output is the next one's input. (1) Slope Stability: an infinite-slope model computing the Factor of Safety from effective cohesion, effective friction angle, slope angle, soil unit weight and the pore-pressure ratio, split into a temporal model that drives soil saturation and pore-water pressure from daily historical rainfall through a bucket hydrology scheme and is validated against recorded landslide events, and a spatial model that runs the same calculation Switzerland-wide to find unstable pixels and, crucially, to output the additional effective cohesion MICP would have to supply - a direct, quantitative target the wet lab can be measured against. Root cohesion is modelled as a parallel natural source, with scenarios for bare soil, roots, MICP and roots plus MICP; the modelled unstable share falls from 82.8% to 28.9% under combined roots and MICP, stabilising 65.04% of initially unstable pixels. (2) Reactive Transport: an adaptation of the Razbani et al. model in PHREEQC, simulating a 52 cm sand column as ten stacked cells with bacteria pre-attached to grains and a urea/CaCl2 cementation solution pumped from below over ~52 hours, using Michaelis-Menten ureolysis kinetics (Rmax, Km, initial reactive surface area, biomass decay time td) and calcite precipitation rate constants k1 = 1.55e-6 and k2 = 0.501 mol m-2 s-1, reproducing both continuous-flow and stop-flow experiments; run with the wet lab's own recipe (1.015 M urea, 2 M CaCl2) it showed more than 2 M CaCl2 brings no benefit, and it predicts 77-79% of lab calcite still forms at 4 C, identifying acidic pH rather than temperature as the bigger obstacle. (3) MICP Feasibility: a binary suitability classification in QGIS combining public Swiss soil and terrain layers on stone content, water storage capacity, permeability and slope, giving 67.06% of Switzerland as technically feasible, then overlaid on landslide hazard and on the stability output to produce a MICP Injection Map - 67.32% of modelled unstable pixels fall inside feasible areas. (4) Economic: unstable cells (FoS <= 1) become release areas fed into the open-source Flow-Py gravitational mass-flow model, producing a runout envelope of 425.2 km2 from 568,627 release cells in the mpp = 1.0 scenario (62.0% of canton Glarus, 348.7-425.2 km2 across tested hydrological conditions); historical landslide frequencies and damage costs then give expected annual damage per asset class (roads, buildings, railways, forests, agricultural land), and tracing the highest-damage locations back to their contributing release areas says where treatment would pay. Combined roots and MICP lower estimated annual damage from CHF 583,000 to CHF 351,000, a 39.8% reduction. A directed evolution strand runs alongside, aimed at a non-GMO second strain.

**datascience.** Their strongest data-science moment is a debugging story they chose to publish. The adapted PHREEQC model initially would not run at all, failing with 'Model failed to converge for initial solution 0'; raising iteration counts, changing tolerances and step size and improving initial guesses did nothing, and removing the calcite-equilibrium constraint made it converge to a physically absurd pH of 1.5. They computed the charge balance at fixed pH from 1 to 12, found it never reached zero, inspected the species and discovered ammonium was almost entirely in its neutral form (5.67e-2 M Amm against 8e-11 M AmmH+) because the reaction AmmH+ = Amm + H+ in the phreeqc.dat database carried no equilibrium constant, so PHREEQC set it to 0 instead of about -9.25; they fixed it with the parameters of the database's own NH4+ = NH3 + H+ reaction. The stated lesson - always check the values a model produces, not just the absence of errors - is the reusable part. The rest of the pipeline is integration work: joining national rainfall records, landslide inventories, digital elevation models, land cover and soil property rasters into one framework, validating predicted instability against recorded events and against SilvaProtect, running sensitivity analyses, and carrying each model's limitations on its own page.

**dataviz.** The modelling work is presented as a prototype decision tool, not a figure dump. An Integrated Dashboard connects slope stability, MICP feasibility, rainfall and potential damage into a single interactive surface for deployment planning, and the team is unusually honest about its state: it currently covers slope stability and selected treatment scenarios and does not yet integrate all four models, so it is labelled a prototype of the intended end-user tool. The model landing page leads with four headline numbers (-53.9% unstable area, 67.06% of Switzerland feasible, 67.32% overlap, -39.8% annual damage, 77-79% calcite at 4 C) each linked to the model that produced it, with arrow navigation between models. Supporting visuals are decision-oriented rather than decorative: unstable share and p95 pore-pressure by canton (which ties instability to the cantonal offices that actually do prevention planning), seasonal cohesion requirements, a required-cohesion histogram, sensitivity analysis, an agreement map against the SilvaProtect reference dataset, and per-asset risk maps for roads, railways, buildings, forest and agricultural land. Derivations are offered as downloadable PDFs (infinite-slope FoS, critical saturation, bucket model) so the maths can be checked independently. An Awards page states plainly which awards the team is claiming and summarises the evidence for each.

**software.** Code is published: the rainfall-triggered slope instability and MICP modelling at https://github.com/Alizzie/RainfallTriggeredSlopeInstabilityMICP, with the team repository at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/uzurich. They did not build a standalone released application; the deliverables are the four validated models, the nationwide MICP Feasibility Map and MICP Injection Map (which they note did not previously exist for Switzerland in any public form), and the Integrated Dashboard prototype on the wiki. They also published a measurement framework for MICP experiments - biological screening, calcium measurement, powder recovery and soil analysis as several independent readouts rather than one, with assay limitations and validation checks documented so future teams can interpret MICP experiments more reliably.

**ihp.** The interview process itself is the method: prepare (write down why this person, what you hope to learn, which assumptions you want tested, and how their input could change SeisMIC), interview with enough flexibility to follow unexpected leads, then reflect back in an interview log on what actually changed, what challenged an assumption, what new concern it raised and who to speak to next. Stakeholders were mapped on a power-interest matrix used to decide how to approach each one rather than to rank importance, and ELSI was treated as a connected framework rather than three boxes. Concrete changes: a researcher told them to start from the environment rather than the organism rather than defaulting to E. coli because it is well characterised. A pore-scale fluid dynamics researcher listed the parameters no MICP model should omit (temperature, pH, oxygen, ion and calcite concentrations, urea hydrolysis, water saturation) and recommended sensitivity analysis to find which dominate - so they dropped a machine learning idea rather than spending the summer discovering it could not be trained, moved the reactive transport work onto established software instead of a custom implementation, and added the sensitivity analysis. Dr. Joaquin Jimenez-Martinez's feedback changed how they treat temperature, bacterial survival and pH. Stakeholders and their PIs repeatedly asking how much vegetation already contributes is why root cohesion was added to the stability model. A microbiologist corrected their premise directly - ammonia release makes soil more basic, not acidic - sending them back to locate the real problem, and suggested reading pH change around colonies with plate indicators; another suggested nitrification inhibitors to stop nitrate forming. An expert pointed out that innovative biological methods usually fail on political opposition rather than feasibility, technology or financing, and suggested they also consider protected natural areas. They dropped CLIMADA after Prof. David Bresch's guidance and reframed the economic benefit as fewer slope failures. Residents below the slopes said what they value most is the surrounding nature, which made the ecological cost of the treatment something to investigate rather than assume; their hesitation about engineered bacteria eased once biomineralisation was explained as a natural process, which told the team their job is explaining the mechanism rather than defending the idea.

**publicEngagement.** Education was run as a two-way exchange explicitly tied to the values the team set in its Human Practices work - transparency, honesty, communication and collaboration - and they state that those became practical criteria for how they communicated rather than abstract principles. Social media carried three recurring formats: 'What even is...?' deep dives into a single concept, 'Word of the Week' introducing one piece of terminology at a time without burying readers in project detail, and 'Myth vs. Fact' separating common assumptions about bacteria, biotechnology and climate change from what the evidence supports. In-person work included an Activity Fair stand and workshops, plus ZurichLernt, and across every activity they tried to distinguish three things for their audience: what is already known, what their own project demonstrated, and what they could not investigate within the time and resources available. They brought in a strategic communication professional to test their assumptions about how to build a campaign, since nobody on the team had communications training.

**realWorld.** The business case is built on a gap they verified rather than assumed: many at-risk Swiss slopes get no protection because concrete and anchors are disproportionate to the risk, and two cantons, Lucerne and Glarus, independently described exactly such slopes. Interviews with Marco Peyer (Risktec) and Prof. David Bresch (ETH Zurich) moved them off insurers and onto the real decision chain - the canton decides and pays, an engineering office proposes the method, the federal government co-finances - so the customer is cantonal natural-hazard offices and their consulting engineers. The offer is deliberately a bundle: a site-specific treatment delivered together with the modelling that shows how much damage it avoids, because as Ulrich Kaiser pointed out, prevention has a visibility problem - a stabilised slope produces no event, no headline and no credit, while the cost is immediate and concrete, so proving avoided damage has to be part of the product. Interest is reported honestly as interest, not sales: one canton offered to connect them with a suitable slope and another asked to follow the damage model, with the team stating plainly that neither is a customer yet. The roadmap is about five to eight years from lab to a first slope, with Swiss approval staged as lab, then field trial, then market. Risks are named with mitigations: urea run-off requires rinsing (one company converts the run-off to fertiliser) and they are investigating a lower-urea route while stating nothing is settled at field scale; containment is handled by a kill switch plus a second strain adapted by directed evolution without genetic engineering.

**給 GEMS：** Steal their interview discipline, which needs no equipment: before every expert conversation write down why this person, what you hope to learn, which assumption you want tested and how their answer could change the project, then log afterwards what actually changed and who to talk to next - that single loop is what let them kill an untrainable machine learning idea in one conversation instead of losing a summer to it. Their published PHREEQC debugging story is the second lesson worth printing on the wall: a model that runs without errors can still be wrong, so check the values, not just the exit code.

### Eton-College-UK — ProteaSign
High School · United Kingdom · https://2026.igem.wiki/eton-college-uk/
ProteaSign is a disposable-cartridge electrochemical diagnostic that separately measures MMP-9 (which degrades the extracellular matrix) and human neutrophil elastase (which degrades the growth factors needed for repair) in chronic wound fluid, turning wound assessment from a visual judgement into a measurement. The sensing interface is a gold electrode carrying methylene-blue-labelled, protease-cleavable peptides whose cleavage is read by square-wave voltammetry, with an independently anchored ferrocene reporter providing internal ratiometric normalisation and a matched non-cleavable peptide control on a second working electrode. The peptide sequences were not guessed: the team built a seven-protease machine-learning substrate predictor trained on 10,472 curated cleavage windows, and validated the predictions with two reprogrammable recombinant sfGFP protease biosensors. It won on the rare combination of genuinely publication-grade dry lab (cluster-aware cross-validation, Laplace-transform kinetics derivations, a physics-based SWV forward model), working hardware, and a human practices programme with over twenty named clinical and industrial stakeholders that visibly moved the design.

**frameworks.** Three distinct modelling efforts, all unusually deep for high school. (1) A protease substrate predictor: for each of seven proteases (MMP-2, MMP-8, MMP-9, MMP-14, neutrophil elastase, LasB, and a pooled digestive serine protease group) they trained two additive scorers on 8-residue cleavage windows — an L2-regularised logistic regression on VHSE physicochemical descriptors (8 descriptors per residue, so 64 standardised features) and a BLOSUM62-smoothed position-specific scoring matrix — using 10,472 confirmed windows from MEROPS, Eckhard et al. 2016 proteomic MMP profiling, and a re-extracted LasB elastin-digestion table from Yang et al. 2015. Negatives were constructed 3:1 (half other proteases' real windows, half random Swiss-Prot 8-mers at natural amino-acid frequencies). (2) A surface-bound enzyme kinetics model: they derived both the steady-state solution and the exact biexponential solution for Michaelis-Menten kinetics on a surface-attached substrate using Laplace transforms and partial-fraction decomposition, then proved analytically and numerically that the steady-state approximation is only valid as their single parameter lambda approaches 1. (3) A square-wave voltammetry forward model (swv_forward_model.py) that computes net SWV current from probe-level physics — about 3.1e10 probes at 7.4 nm spacing, with a 1.4 nm methylene-blue lateral excursion used to justify treating probes as non-interacting.

**datascience.** The evaluation methodology is the real achievement and is more careful than most undergraduate iGEM dry lab. They recognised that near-duplicate cleavage windows cause data leakage under ordinary K-fold CV, so they defined Hamming-distance clusters (any pair with d_H <= 2, taken as connected components, found in near-linear time via a 3+3+2-block pigeonhole trick with union-find) and used stratified group 5-fold splitting whole clusters, with a nested 3-fold inner CV to pick the regularisation strength C per protease, and the null percentile distribution and PSSM rebuilt per outer fold to avoid leaking into the background. They separated two questions — Detection (held-out positives vs random background) and Discrimination (held-out positives vs another protease's confirmed sites), noting the latter is what actually matters for a multiplexed sensor. They derived and Monte-Carlo-verified an analytic ceiling on measured AUROC under false negatives (measured AUROC <= 1 - pi/2 for a fraction pi of mislabelled negatives), ran three controls (label shuffle collapsing AUROC to 0.49-0.53; composition-only ablation showing e.g. 0.664 vs 0.874 for MMP-2 but 0.886 vs 0.877 for LasB because 76% of its positives come from elastin; and random vs cluster-aware folds, where LasB drops 0.886 to 0.879 once leakage is removed). Scores from the two models are converted to percentiles against 100,000 random Swiss-Prot background windows so they are comparable across proteases, combined by harmonic mean (high only when both are high), and reported as a 'specificity margin' = target consensus percentile minus the strongest competitor's. They also published an explicit list of eight assumptions and limitations, including that additivity costs at most 0.007 AUROC against gradient-boosted trees, that VHSE PCA captures only 64-79% of the full positional signal, and that the harmonic-mean consensus was reasoned rather than validated.

**dataviz.** The substrate predictor page ends in a live in-browser scorer ('Try It — Score a Peptide'): you type a peptide, mark the scissile bond, and every protease in the panel scores it as you type, with warm/cool per-position attribution bars that sum exactly to the logit and the PSSM score, and grey bars for unknown (gapped) positions. The sensor probe itself is shown scored at every bond by the MMP-9 and elastase models, with the P4-to-P4' window shaded and the actual cut marked. The SWV page carries an interactive forward-model plot where moving across reads every predicted current curve at one potential. Results are presented as out-of-fold ROC curves, precision-recall curves against a 0.25 prior, and held-out percentile distributions against a uniform null, plus paired difference plots with 95% cluster-bootstrap intervals where a filled marker means the interval excludes zero. Equations are rendered in KaTeX and the human practices page uses globe.gl.

**software.** The substrate predictor is released as a protease-agnostic Python package (modules spred.data, spred.model, spred.pssm, spred.train, spred.validation, spred.evaluation, spred.panel) that another team retrains on its own protease panel's known substrates on a basic laptop in a few hours; the team explicitly frames it as a reusable contribution. Hardware: a handheld reader built around the Analog Devices AD5940 electrochemical analogue front end with an nRF52840 microcontroller and a TI TMUX1104 4:1 precision multiplexer, sequentially interrogating four working electrodes against a shared reference and counter electrode, with full KiCad schematics (5 sheets) and an exported bill of materials released as PDF. The hardware builds on the open-source Biocoin wearable multiplexed biosensing platform (github.com/ProfDrewHall/Biocoin; Hack & Hall, npj Biosensing 2026). They also contribute two reprogrammable recombinant protease biosensors with swappable substrate 'cassettes': pES-01 (FLAG-sfGFP / peptide / C-terminal His6, read by Ni-NTA depletion, ELISA, Western blot or SDS-PAGE) and pDUAL (split-sfGFP with GFP11 embedded in an eglin c surface loop, giving a fluorescence readout). Code and wiki at https://gitlab.igem.org/2026/eton-college-uk.

**ihp.** Over twenty named stakeholders across wound care, electrochemistry, health economics, regulation and patient advocacy, with a 'pinpoint / event / action' structure that states what changed. Concrete examples: Dr Anatoliy Markiv (King's College London) moved them off pET-24a(+) to pSB1C3 as a reusable starting plasmid, reviewed their primers and proposed a better substrate-swapping method, and pointed them to the split-GFP protease-sensing paper that became their second design cycle; he also required construct sequences for biosafety assessment before permitting experiments. Dr Ben Bullen (podiatry) cemented the reusable-reader / disposable-cartridge split and the ~20 microlitre sample volume, and set a 15-minute workflow target against the team's estimated 30 minutes — which the team records as an unmet goal requiring shorter incubation. Ms Kathleen Leak (tissue viability) and Trish Idensohn drove the requirement for fast readouts and simple operating procedures, which produced the cartridge's standardised metering, dilution and incubation steps before SWV acquisition. Dr Honda Hsu (plastic surgeon, Taiwan) confirmed the device fits a real clinical workflow and his account of delegated wound care created an explicit usability requirement that routine dressing-change staff, not just specialists, must be able to run it. Dr Kevin Lye (Accorto Regulatory Solutions) and Dr Douglas Queen (health economics of wound care) covered the regulatory and reimbursement path; Dr Martin Peacock (Zimmer and Peacock) and Professor Kevin Lam (synthetic electrochemistry, Greenwich) and Dr Ana Maria Totea advised on electrodes and liquid handling; Professor Keith Harding (Cardiff), Professor Steven Jeffery (Pioneer Wound Clinics), Professor Dato Harikrishna Nair, Professor Paul Davis (co-founder of Mologic) and Professor Eleanor Stride (Oxford biomedical engineering) reviewed the clinical and device case. Patient and charity voices included 'Bob', a person living with a chronic wound, Breakthrough T1D and Diabetes Scotland. Feedback also reinforced measuring cleavage rate with calibration across known enzyme concentrations. The anonymised 'David' narrative on the description page is explicitly constructed from real accounts heard through these conversations.

**publicEngagement.** A genuinely reusable education portfolio rather than a set of one-off visits. 'What If?' is a team-written and illustrated comic modelled on Marvel's What If...? series, built directly from the four ideas children drew at the Eton Porny workshop (colour-changing plants, bacteria making medicines, programmable cells, healing wounds); over 350 printed copies were distributed in two months and it was translated into two further languages. A 58-page Activities Handbook of printable exercises at graded difficulty, with instructions and answer keys written in conversation with a secondary school teacher, was inspired by Leiden iGEM 2025's approach to reusable materials. 'Bio-Detectives' is a museum-sabotage mystery workshop for Year 8 in which teams work five stations — reconstructing DNA sequences, exploring protein production, critiquing flawed experiments, comparing lab labels, and modelling genetic control through AND/OR/NOR gates — and must explain their reasoning to unlock each piece of evidence, ending in a fixed-budget redesign task; student and facilitator packs plus the presentation are released so it can be rerun. Year 11 volunteers facilitated and reported their own gains ('I'm not a science student but still really enjoyed it because of the mystery format'). They report honestly that the content was too hard for pupils who had not yet met DNA and recommend targeting Year 10/11 instead. Other sessions: a hands-on goat-DNA genetic modification build for 34 Year 5 pupils at St George's Windsor (physically assembling glowing / curly-hair / spider-silk gene templates from spare nucleotides), an edible animal-cell modelling workshop with a published allergen risk assessment, protease kits for a carers' workshop, street interviews (8 of N respondents had no personal experience of chronic wounds), and biosafety videos.

**realWorld.** The implementation page is a structured device risk assessment rather than a business pitch: it enumerates infection transfer through reusable components, pain or damage to fragile healing tissue, allergic reaction to wound-contacting materials, unnecessary anxiety or treatment escalation from false positives, and exposure of identifiable patient data, each with a named mitigation (prefer single-use patient-contacting components, biocompatibility assessment of all wound-contacting materials, clinically justified interpretation criteria with evaluated specificity and false-positive rates, calibration and quality-control procedures with error alerts and clear invalid-test instructions, minimised personal data collection with access restriction and retention policies). The intended route to market is a reusable reader plus disposable cartridge for community wound care — GPs, wound-care nurses, podiatrists and carers — positioned to guide selection of the existing protease-modulating dressings (e.g. UrgoStart) and to track proteolytic activity over time alongside wound size. Costing came from the KiCad bill of materials plus estimated enclosure and reagent costs. The team is candid that clinical validation, bacterial confounding of the chosen peptides, and testing on real clinical samples all remain outstanding. A Smith + Nephew work experience business insight day and an Imperial iGEM mini-jamboree (24 August, UK and European teams) fed the commercial framing.

**給 GEMS：** Copy their evaluation discipline, not just their model: before reporting any ML metric, cluster near-duplicate sequences by Hamming distance and split whole clusters across folds, then run a label-shuffle control and an ablation that strips the information you claim to be using — three cheap steps that turn a high-school classifier from a number into evidence. Their second transferable move is shipping the model as a live in-browser scorer with per-position attribution bars, so a judge or clinician can interrogate the prediction instead of taking the AUROC on trust.

### UCNZ — NanoBrew
Undergrad · New Zealand · https://2026.igem.wiki/ucnz/
NanoBrew takes brewers' spent grain (BSG), which makes up about 85% of beer brewing waste by weight and is mostly landfilled or sold as cheap animal feed, and extracts nanocellulose from it enzymatically instead of with hot acid and energy-intensive mechanical grinding. The team expressed a Bacillus subtilis xylanase (XynA) to strip hemicellulose and open up the cellulose, plus an ancestrally reconstructed Cel5A endoglucanase fused to a carbohydrate binding module to cut cellulose down to nanofibrils, and tested six construct variants with and without the YebF secretion tag in E. coli. It was Top 10 and nominated for Presentation, Entrepreneurship and Biomanufacturing because the project is framed end to end as a New Zealand circular-economy story - built on a real brewery partnership, grounded in the Maori value of kaitiakitanga, with a full pilot-plant cost analysis and letters of support - and because the team is candid that it never managed to characterise its product. No previous iGEM team had extracted nanocellulose from lignocellulosic plant material rather than growing it bacterially.

**frameworks.** Modest but purposeful, and honestly scoped. Before ordering genes, all six constructs were folded with AlphaFold 3 and the predicted structures aligned in PyMOL against the unfused enzymes to check the YebF tag, linkers and CBM had not disturbed the catalytic core - RMSD came out at 0.101 and 0.117 Angstrom for XynA and YebF-XynA, and 0.183, 0.155, 0.173 Angstrom for the endoglucanase variants, all well under 2 Angstrom, with pTM reported per model and the flexible linker correctly flagged as an unstructured region. Enzyme assays were run as time-series DNS and fitted to Michaelis-Menten-like behaviour on both the control substrate (birchwood xylan) and on BSG, with enzyme inactivation used to freeze each timepoint. For the system-level question they built a causal loop diagram with 12 nodes linking the environmental, economic and social effects of an upscaled process, signed each causal link positive or negative, and decomposed the graph into balancing and reinforcing loops - while explicitly refusing to quantify link strength. The microfluidic viscometer was designed entirely in simulation (Capillarix, an unreleased capillary-microfluidics simulator supplied by its creator) with a simulated error table, and the absorbance sensor uses a machine learning calibration running on the device itself.

**datascience.** The dry lab's strongest quality is calibrated honesty rather than volume of computation. The team states plainly at the top of the entrepreneurship page that its market research targeted cellulose nanofibrils because that was the anticipated product from the literature, but that it was unable to characterise what it actually made; the FTIR comparison against a pure nanocellulose reference sample came back inconclusive, and they published that, named ATR-FTIR as the next attempt, and said they were waiting on expert advice as of the wiki freeze. For the absorbance sensor they ran out of nanocellulose and substituted guar gum, justifying it as shear-thinning with a similar concentration-opacity relationship, and tabulating the results as such. The viscometer error table notes that surface roughness is not modelled. They also report that only one student in their school talks had heard of iGEM, and that a 2019 survey of 9,000 New Zealanders found 30% opposed selling GM food at all - using measured baselines rather than assertions about public attitudes.

**dataviz.** The two devices are the visualization story: the project needed a way to read nanocellulose concentration from microlitre samples, and the engineering subteam built it. The differential microfluidic viscometer compares a sample against a reference fluid in a sealed channel to cancel out the variable hydrophilicity of PMMA, computing relative viscosity as the ratio of average length-times-velocity products over the first second of flow, then calibrating to the expected sample range so unknowns are read by linear interpolation. The optical sensor strobes red, green and blue LEDs sequentially and feeds the three absorbance values to a machine learning model on an onboard ESP32, which infers concentration - and is deliberately built so a biotechnologist can recalibrate it for whatever property they want to infer. The wiki itself keeps each page to a clear sectioned structure with a sidebar contents list, and the stakeholder work is presented as an influence-interest grid rather than a list.

**software.** No standalone software release. The hardware is the deliverable: two sensors for reading nanocellulose concentration in microlitre volumes, one a differential capillary-microfluidics viscometer validated in simulation, the other a built RGB-strobing absorbance/turbidity sensor with on-ESP32 machine learning calibration, both developed through two documented iterations of the engineering design cycle and integrated into University of Canterbury engineering students' coursework with some of those students joining as external collaborators. Parts are the other contribution: six constructs registered, with EG-CBM (BBa_26TOG7XZ) highlighted as expressing and purifying extremely well with good activity on complex substrates, plus Pichia/yeast-targeted versions using an OST1 signal sequence and T2A self-cleaving peptide bicistronic designs (BBa_266IKFQ3, BBa_26OB3D76), and a characterisation of the YebF secretion tag (BBa_K1610300, from TAS_Taipei 2015) intended to let future teams choose a secretion system on evidence.

**ihp.** Human practices is organised around kaitiakitanga, the Maori concept of guardianship, with Bree Bell (Kaiarahi for UC Science) consulted early on how the project interfaces with iwi and hapu, and further consultation explicitly deferred to the scale-up stage rather than claimed as done. Stakeholders are mapped on an influence-interest grid and the design changes are specific. The team was split between on-site plants at each brewery and one centralised facility; Professor Jack Heinemann and Dr Brigitta Kurenbach, both involved in international synthetic biology regulation, argued that a distributed model multiplies accidental-exposure risk and regulatory burden because each site needs separate approval, so the team went centralised. The same pair identified the circular-economy rebound effect - if BSG becomes valuable, beer gets cheaper to make, production rises and total waste could increase - and told them 'sustainable' depends on timeframe and is often marketing; the team consequently narrowed its claim to reducing environmental impact relative to alternative BSG disposal, up to a stated horizon, and no further. Materially Kiwi (a startup making leather from kiwifruit waste) independently warned that customers buy on performance, consistency and price, not sustainability, and that a free feedstock does not mean a cheap product once collection, processing, testing and equipment are counted - which moved yield confirmation and full process costing to the top of the priority list. Dr Stefan Hill and Dr Mathias Sorieul at the Bioeconomy Science Institute warned that BSG-derived nanocellulose may be indistinguishable from wood-derived, so the low-cost waste feedstock, not the material, is the selling point; they also reframed BSG's high hemicellulose as a possible advantage, citing an Australian spinifex grass result where hemicellulose remnants improved material properties, and prescribed the three characterisation methods (SEM for fibril width, sedimentation for aspect ratio, FTIR for purity) the team then attempted. Dr Andrew Prest at Foodstuffs Own Brands listed what a packaging buyer needs and confirmed food-contact use would need substantial safety assessment, which is why the team targets non-food packaging first. Lincoln Agritech's suggestion of rheology as a measurement route is what started the viscometer, and Professor Volker Nock was met at the BIC symposium after researchers there raised the energy cost of freeze-thaw cycles at scale.

**publicEngagement.** Outreach was built around a deliberate hypothesis: in New Zealand, synthetic biology means genetic modification and genetic modification means risk, so the team tested whether a local story changes how people engage. They gave three secondary-school talks (one at Burnside High School, two at Christchurch Girls' High School, both schools some members had attended) covering synthetic biology, iGEM, what a science degree looks like and how NanoBrew works, and structured them for dialogue - long question time, small-group breakout discussion, a quiz where answers were argued through rather than marked, contact details left for follow-ups, and teacher feedback collected. Their findings are reported as findings: students already knew breweries and brewery waste so the local hook carried the science; small groups worked far better than whole-cohort presentation; most questions were about science careers and preparing for university, where undergraduates were better placed to answer than any teacher; and only one student had ever heard of iGEM. For the wider public they worked with the university communications team on a press release framed as a local problem with a local solution, which reached The Press, NZ Herald, Radio New Zealand, NewstalkZB, The Breeze, The Platform and deliberately rural and regional outlets including the Ashburton Courier and Selwyn Times, with a team member and the PI giving radio interviews that explained containment in plain language; the Instagram account passed 23,000 views. They also presented at the Biomolecular Interaction Centre Winter Symposium. The published lessons for future teams are practical: get your institution's comms team involved early, and contact schools months ahead because they plan a year out.

**realWorld.** The commercial case is unusually complete for an undergraduate team and backed by two letters of support (Cassels Brewing Co. and Lincoln University). Local grounding: in Christchurch alone BSG accounts for an estimated 680-1,000 tonnes to landfill a year, costing breweries up to NZ$220,000 in disposal fees, and nationally roughly 13,700 tonnes to landfill producing 14,000 tonnes CO2-equivalent, which the promotional video renders as 3,300 petrol cars running for a year. Market: nanocellulose at US$947 million in 2026 growing at 23.74% CAGR to a projected US$6.4 billion by 2035, with the team noting that estimates vary between reports and stating which figure it uses throughout. Price reality from stakeholders sets the strategy: at around $100/kg nanocellulose suits high-value medical uses while broad uptake needs roughly $10/kg, so packaging is the entry market. The page carries a development roadmap, a commercial-scale cost forecast, a downloadable preliminary CNF cost analysis for a pilot-scale plant, financial analysis and timeline, a business exit strategy, minimum viable product definition, PEST, SWOT, risk and competitor analyses (including Nano-Sea/AgriSea making kelp-derived nanocellulose locally, which does not target packaging), and a pitch deck. On IP, the UC Technology Transfer Office told them a first filing runs NZ$10-15K and is only worth it if results look promising, that only novel elements need protecting, that much of their approach is already published so finding the novel element may be hard, and that they should BLAST their enzyme sequences against patented sequences to check freedom to operate - and that they should document negative results because that is how an invention's origin is evidenced. The team notes everything submitted to iGEM enters the public domain, so any filing had to precede the wiki. Continuation is real: the media coverage plus the results won University of Canterbury funding for a summer research project carrying the work on under Dr Kelsi Hall, one of only 18 scholarships awarded across all faculties in 2026. The team also commits to licensing the process to other agricultural and food-processing waste streams once protected, with documentation, stakeholder map and methods open now.

**給 GEMS：** UCNZ shows how to publish an unfinished result well: they never characterised their nanocellulose, said so at the top of the page that depended on it, named the failed method (FTIR, inconclusive against a reference sample), the planned replacement (ATR-FTIR) and the substitute material they used when samples ran out - and still won Top 10. The second transferable move is the local hook: anchor the project in an industry students already recognise, then get the institution's communications office involved early enough that national and regional media carry the story, which is what converted their outreach into continuation funding.

### HongKong-HS — AmpliRen - a urine-based home screening kit concept for chronic kidney disease using urinary miRNA and hybridisation chain reaction
High School · Hong Kong · https://2026.igem.wiki/hongkong-hs/
HongKong-HS is a five-school joint team (Wah Yan College Kowloon, Pope Paul VI College, C&MA Sun Kei Secondary School, Tsung Tsin Christian Academy, St. Paul's School Lam Tin) tackling chronic kidney disease, which affects roughly 788 million adults worldwide, has risen past 405,000 recorded adult cases in Hong Kong, and is usually caught only at stage 3-5 because creatinine-based eGFR does not move until about half of kidney function is gone. AmpliRen detects two urinary microRNAs - miR-21-5p for fibrosis severity and miR-192-5p as an early warning, together reported at 89% sensitivity and 82% specificity - and amplifies the signal enzyme-free at room temperature with hybridisation chain reaction, whose G-rich hairpin loops fold into G-quadruplexes that bind hemin to form a DNAzyme and oxidise TMB into a colour change visible in natural light. The project is a genuine four-cycle engineering story: the team started with toehold switches designed in miRADAR and screened in NUPACK, found EGFP output too weak and invisible, pivoted to HCR, then to G-quadruplex-containing probes, then to hemin/TMB colorimetry. It was nominated for Best Wiki on one of the most ambitious scroll-driven, 3D-visualised wikis in the competition.

**frameworks.** The dry lab is nucleic-acid thermodynamics rather than protein design, and it is used as a hard screen at every cycle. Candidate toehold switches were generated with miRADAR, the design tool released by the 2024 Wageningen iGEM team - a deliberate reuse of another team's software rather than reinventing it - producing 9 candidates for miR-21-5p and 7 for miR-192-5p. Every candidate was then simulated in NUPACK (RNA mode, 37 C, default model options and algorithm settings, 1 uM toehold and 3 uM miRNA to keep the trigger in excess) and scored against five explicit criteria: bound-toehold equilibrium concentration, absence of unintended secondary structure downstream of the ribosome binding site (which would block the ribosome and cause false negatives), hybrid minimum free energy (HMFE) versus toehold minimum free energy (TMFE) so that the bound state is thermodynamically favoured and the switch does not prefer to dimerise with another switch, C-G content for hairpin stability, and RBS location. They tabulated the HMFE-TMFE difference for every candidate in kcal/mol and read NUPACK's base-pair equilibrium-probability plots to check that loop-maintaining base pairs drop to low probability on target binding so the switch can fully linearise - selecting toeholds 6 and 7 for miR-192-5p and 7 and 9 for miR-21-5p. The same NUPACK workflow was then reapplied to HCR: H1/H2 hairpin pairs (the miR-21-5p pair adopted from Miao et al. 2016, the miR-192-5p pair built in house) were simulated at 37 C with 1 uM hairpin and 3 uM miRNA, confirming long H1-H2 polymer formation with target but also predicting unintended H1-H2 binding in the absence of target - a background-leakage problem the model found before the gel did. Minimum-free-energy structures were computed for H1 alone, H2 alone, H1+miRNA and the full miRNA-H1-H2 complex for both targets. In Cycle 4, double-loop G4H1/G4H2 hairpins based on Peng et al. (2022) had InG4 G-quadruplex motifs inserted into the loops, and NUPACK was used to confirm both complex formation and that the InG4 sequences sit in the loops where they can fold and leave the polymer after HCR. The two probe pairs were deliberately given different geometries - longer stems and smaller loops for miR-192-5p, shorter stems and larger loops for miR-21-5p.

**datascience.** Analysis is modest in volume but correctly specified. Cell-free EGFP expression was compared with and without target miRNA across five repeats against both positive controls (pET-14b-EGFP with no toehold) and no-plasmid negative controls, read on a fluorometer at 488 nm excitation and 507-513 nm emission, with significance tested by one-sample t-test on fold change; the honest outcome was that miR-21 candidates showed no significant difference, miR-192-5p-6 was significant but minimal at 1.03-fold, and miR-192-5p-7 showed a more pronounced 1.51-fold increase that did not reach significance - and they reported that rather than spin it. ThT fluorescence and hemin/TMB colorimetric assays were analysed by one-way ANOVA with Dunnett post-hoc against the 0 pM control: miR-21 gave significant signal at 100 pM, 10 nM and 100 nM (n=3, p<0.001), while miR-192 was significant at 100 nM (p=0.01 and p=0.002) but also, unexpectedly, significantly lower than control at 1 nM - an anomaly they diagnosed as free miR-192-5p G4H1 self-folding into a G-quadruplex and producing colour without target, and then turned into a concrete future-work list (splitting the G4, stabilising the hairpin stem, tuning C-G/A-T content, optimising toehold length). Plasmid work was confirmed by Sanger sequencing and miniprep A260/280 purity, and gel evidence was escalated from agarose to PAGE when agarose smearing proved inconclusive.

**dataviz.** The wiki itself is the data-visualisation achievement and is why it was nominated for Best Wiki. The landing page is a scroll-driven narrative that zooms from two kidneys, through tissue and the filtration barrier, down to the molecular signal, with each stage labelled as an illustrative view rather than clinical eGFR categories. The HCR mechanism is animated across four scroll states - two locked hairpins, target binding and toehold opening, chain growth into a double-stranded nanowire, then potassium-dependent G-quadruplex folding with hemin - so a reader physically watches the amplification cascade instead of reading a paragraph about it. Epidemiology is presented as individually sourced stat cards, each carrying its own population, year and citation (788 million adults globally, GBD 2023/The Lancet 2025; 87% unaware, CDC 2026 NHANES 2021-2023; 405,833 Hong Kong adult cases 2021, Yue et al.; 2,571 on the transplant waiting list; 1,226 registered deaths in 2024) with an explicit note that one figure is a recorded-case count, not a current population estimate. The kit concept is presented as an interactive unboxing with three fitted compartments and a pannable close-up, and the team labels it openly as AI-assisted imagery and animation made with Higgsfield and as a research concept, not a validated diagnostic product. The engineering page is built as a clickable 22-note timeline across four Design-Build-Test-Learn cycles. Every figure carries a full descriptive caption and alt text.

**software.** No standalone software or hardware was released. The dry lab is the application of existing tools - NUPACK for thermodynamic simulation and another iGEM team's miRADAR for candidate generation - plus a bespoke wiki front end. Two toehold switch candidates per target were cloned into pET-14b-EGFP using XbaI and NdeI sites between the T7 promoter and the EGFP reporter and verified by Sanger sequencing, and an mCherry colorimetric variant was in progress when the season ended.

**ihp.** IHP was organised as four parallel two-way feedback loops (Public, Healthcare, Science, Industry) feeding both the wet lab and the education team, structured over three stages (Understanding the Problem, Identifying the Needs, Develop & Co-design) and processed through a four-step cycle they call LIVP (Locate, Iterate, Validate, Propose). The design changes are traceable to named people. Professor Chan Ting Fung (RNA biology) assessed the toehold-switch limitations and identified HCR as the alternative worth trying for signal amplification - the single biggest pivot in the project - and later recommended expanding the H1/H2 sequence design space to mask the ribosome binding site to eliminate background leakage, noted that lithium interference in urine is negligible, and told them to test sodium's effect on the DNAzyme experimentally. Professor Szeto Cheuk Chun (Head of Medicine and Therapeutics, CUHK, whose research is urinary biomarkers) confirmed miRNA as near-ideal for urine because of its stability, told them to run miR-21-5p and miR-192-5p in parallel as a complementary test (which is why the kit has two detection pathways and a six-well chamber), said biomarkers are detectable in urine that has not been high-speed centrifuged so they could drop centrifugation from the workflow, warned that urinary chromogens may interfere with a visible colour readout, set a user-experience target of roughly half an hour to result, and endorsed a colour change readable under natural light - which is precisely why the team ended up on G4/hemin colorimetry rather than ThT fluorescence, since ThT needs UV excitation and a fluorescence reader.
